content:
Beaumont Hamel British Cemetery is a British war cemetary located in Beaumont-Hamel, a commune in the Somme region in the Hauts-de-France in northern France. It is one of the several cemeteries dedicated to the thousands of British and Commonwealth soldiers who were killed in the Battle of the Somme during the First World War.

The cemetery is maintained and managed by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission, an intergovernmental organization responsible for maintaining, marking, and commemorating Commonwealth war graves around the world.

Beaumont Hamel British Cemetery was initiated on the battlefield after the Armistice in November 1918, gathering graves from the surrounding area. The cemetery currently holds the remains of 179 servicemen from the United Kingdom and 18 from Newfoundland.

Like many other military cemeteries, the graves are marked by uniform headstones, which bear the name, rank, regiment, and date of death of the soldier. They often also contain a personal message from the family or a religious quotation.

The cemetery is small compared to many others in the region. Nonetheless, it stands as a testimony to the massive human cost of the Battle of the Somme, one of the bloodiest battles in human history with over one million casualties.

In addition to individual grave markers, the cemetery and its immediate surroundings are dotted with memorials and monuments dedicated to specific units or individuals. These include the iconic Newfoundland Memorial, which commemorates the Newfoundland Regiment that suffered heavy casualties trying to capture Beaumont-Hamel on the first day of the Battle of the Somme.

Significantly, the Beaumont-Hamel Newfoundland Memorial site is one of only two National Historic Sites of Canada located outside Canada. It pays tribute to the significant participation of Newfoundland soldiers during the First World War.
